title: The Group of Seven
summary: Josh and Chuck (credited in the transcript as the 'iHeart Intro' speaker) explore the Group of Seven, the Canadian painters who formed the foundation of Canada's modern artistic identity. They cover the founding members and precursors such as J.E.H. MacDonald, Tom Thompson, Lawren Harris, A.Y. Jackson, Arthur Lismer, Frederick Varley, Franklin Carmichael and Frank Johnston; the Grip design firm and Arts and Letters Club; Algonquin Park sketching trips and box car journeys; Tom Thompson's mysterious drowning; the 1920 formation and the 1921 show; the 1930s disbandment and expansion into the Canadian Group of Painters; Emily Carr's unofficial membership; and the WWII silkscreen print program. The episode ends with a listener mail correction about fentanyl and Suboxone in prisons.
topics: Eric Brown National Gallery of Canada

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to the Group of Seven
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the Group of Seven as Canada's famous group of painters who worked together and influenced one another, and banter about whether they knew the artists.

segments.title: Canadian national identity and the group's origins
segments.summary: The hosts describe how the group painted Canadian wilderness as the country sought a national identity after Confederation. They note the group formed officially in 1920 after members had worked together in the 1910s, centered in Toronto, and were tied to the Grip design firm and the Arts and Letters Club.

segments.title: J.E.H. MacDonald and Tom Thompson
segments.summary: J.E.H. MacDonald, the oldest member and a father figure, was head designer at the Grip and was frail and often ill. Tom Thompson, never an official member, worked at the Grip, introduced the others to the wilderness, and was a key influence before dying young. MacDonald's painting Missed Fantasy appears in The Shining.

segments.title: Tom Thompson's career and Lawren Harris
segments.summary: Tom Thompson's short career produced about fifty canvases and four hundred sketches before his death at 39. Lawren Harris, a wealthy heir to a British agricultural equipment fortune, is discussed as a painter whose Mountain Forms sold for eleven million dollars and who is seen as possibly the first abstract painter in Canada.

segments.title: Spiritualism and the group's transition to modern painting
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the group's shared spiritual and transcendentalist sensibilities and how their style became more similar over time, representing a transition from traditional to modern painting in Canada.

segments.title: Algonquin Park trips and early sketching
segments.summary: In May 1912 Thompson and Harry B. Jackson traveled by train to Algonquin Provincial Park to sketch. The hosts discuss the radical nature of artists venturing into the wilderness, and Thompson's near-year-round time there. Paintings such as The Jack Pine and A.Y. Jackson's The Red Maple are mentioned.

segments.title: Sketching technique and personal art tangents
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the artists made sketches outdoors and later translated them into canvases. Much of this section is personal banter about Chuck's wife's painting and the hosts' own drawing abilities, plus a tangent about Altoids tins and scrubbing past episodes.

segments.title: European training and the 1912 Scandinavian exhibition
segments.summary: Most members studied in Europe, but found European techniques did not suit the Canadian wilderness. Lawren Harris and J.E.H. MacDonald saw a Scandinavian art exhibition in Buffalo, New York in 1912, which freed them to paint the feeling nature inspired. Vincent van Gogh and impasto technique are also mentioned.

segments.title: Studio Building and patronage
segments.summary: Doctor James McCallum funded the Studio Building in Toronto's Rosedale neighborhood, which provided cheap studio space. McCallum built Tom Thompson a shed and charged him a dollar a month, and the hosts share a 'you're so broke' joke.

segments.title: World War One and dazzle camouflage
segments.summary: World War One delayed the group's formation and many members served or painted for the Canadian War Memorials Fund. Arthur Lismer painted returning warships with dazzle camouflage, a confusing pattern meant to mislead about heading and speed.

segments.title: Tom Thompson's death
segments.summary: Tom Thompson, who worked as a fishing guide and park ranger, died in 1917 after his canoe was found overturned. He was officially ruled an accidental drowning, though some theorize suicide or murder. His death was a major blow to the group.

segments.title: Box car journeys and the Wild River
segments.summary: After MacDonald helped build a memorial cairn at Canoe Lake and suffered a collapse, the group took painting trips in Algoma using a box car Lawren Harris obtained from a railroad, outfitted as a traveling studio. MacDonald painted The Wild River in 1919.

segments.title: First exhibition and formal founding
segments.summary: The group's first exhibition, around 200 canvases, got a mixed reception from critics. In early 1920 they formally formed the group; A.Y. Jackson, who was away sketching, learned of his membership afterward.

segments.title: Group members' backgrounds: A.Y. Jackson, Arthur Lismer, Frederick Varley, Franklin Carmichael, Frank Johnston
segments.summary: The hosts describe the members' backgrounds: A.Y. Jackson's early life, Montreal ties, and World War One service and wounding; Lismer's dazzle camouflage paintings; Varley's wartime work and bombed village paintings; Franklin Carmichael's decorative watercolors; and Frank Johnston's quick watercolor work and name change from Francis Hans Johnston to Franz.

segments.title: Official 1920 exhibition and critical reception
segments.summary: The official unified show opened May 7 at the Art Gallery of Toronto with 120 paintings. Some critics disparaged the work, while the second show in 1921 drew about 2,500 people over three weeks. Eric Brown, director of the National Gallery of Canada, bought works and promoted them, though he was later criticized for not championing women or Indigenous artists.
topics: Eric Brown National Gallery of Canada

segments.title: Expansion: Edwin Holgate, A.J. Casson, LeMoyne FitzGerald and Emily Carr
segments.summary: The group added Edwin Holgate in 1929, a portraitist who had formed the Beaver Hall Group in Montreal, then A.J. Casson, who was Carmichael's assistant, and LeMoyne FitzGerald in 1932. Emily Carr was never an official member but was featured in shows and considered unofficially one of them; she stopped selling Indigenous-style crafts to tourists.

segments.title: Disbandment and Canadian Group of Painters
segments.summary: MacDonald died in 1932 and the group disbanded in 1933 amid pushback over regional and artistic scope. They regrouped as the Canadian Group of Painters, starting with 28 artists and growing to 61, including women.

segments.title: WWII silkscreen prints and national cementing
segments.summary: During World War Two the Canadian government ran a silkscreen print program reproducing the group's art for government buildings, banks and schools, and selling prints. Arthur Lismer helped select images. Critics noted the omission of women, coastal artists and Indigenous artists.

segments.title: Closing thoughts and personal banter
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the Group of Seven website and related art searches, then chat about Chuck's fiftieth birthday approaching and midlife happiness.

segments.title: Listener mail: Suboxone in prisons and fentanyl correction
segments.summary: A listener who teaches in an Indiana correctional facility corrects the hosts: prisons offer Suboxone as treatment, not just drying out. Another listener notes that officers wear gloves during cell searches to avoid fentanyl absorption through skin. The hosts thank Samuel.

segments.summary: Standard closing with iHeartRadio credit and podcast listening information.
